searchText: IIRC (it has been a long time) there are some benefits related to recursive proofs or something. But I think we can't really reap those specific benefits on L1 unless we switch everything to it eventually. I think there are some other benefits in terms of developer ergonomics, but I forget what they are. <@301186049323958275> Hello, I run prysm with geth locally, after I disconnect prysm and geth for few minutes, I found block can't increase, failed to update forkchoice to prepare for new unsafe payload. I think forkchoiceUpdated api was locked. Is it nomal? Why was it happend? I am not the right person to ask, but what you are describing does sound like a potentially serious problem. I recommend asking in the Prysm discord server, as they are best equipped to help you troubleshoot. Thanks a lot. I will try it. Just wrote a backtracking to Ethereum's Finality Challenge 2 weeks ago 😀 https://twitter.com/ChrisYicheng/status/1663177404964302849?s=20 <@211091239112671234> I think given this, it might be easier to reverse the premise in your doc that Version A is simpler than Version B 🙂 Version B lets us "do something before the chain finalizes", and holds as long as the buggy clients represent >33% of the stake I never meant to suggest that A was simpler than B. For me, A holds more unknowns. But yeah, sure, makes sense to do the simplest scenarios first ah, my bad - it felt implied by the "TBD, let's focus on Version A first ." in the doc 😅 Another angle to consider in all of this is making it easy for people to switch clients ASAP if something goes wrong. That can be the difference between 50%+ of the network being on the wrong chain for a week vs. getting the majority of those moved to another client in 1-2 days
